items.title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
items.one_liner: Biomedical claim-verification agent study shows retrieval is the core bottleneck and simple citation existence checks are insufficient.
items.summary: Researchers conducted a controlled ablation study on biomedical claim-verification agents using the SciFact benchmark and the live PubMed API to evaluate harness design. The study demonstrated that while naive single-shot retrieval yields poor recall, letting agents formulate their own queries triples gold recall and achieves 62% accuracy. Furthermore, providing gold abstracts pushes accuracy up to 79–86%, revealing that retrieval quality rather than reasoning is the primary bottleneck. A citation audit also revealed that closed-book models frequently cite existing PubMed IDs that are completely irrelevant, proving that simple existence checks are inadequate safeguards for scientific language agents.
items.bottom_line: Enabling LLM agents to construct their own search queries significantly improves biomedical claim verification, while raw existence checks fail to catch irrelevant citations.

claims.text: Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts, although these differences are not significant at our sample size.
claims.support_span: Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget.

items.title: UserSWE: Evaluating Coding Agents in Multi-Turn Conversations with Dynamic Users
items.one_liner: This framework provides a more realistic evaluation method for AI coding agents by simulating multi-turn developer interactions rather than single-shot code generation.
items.summary: UserSWE is a new benchmark designed to evaluate coding agents in multi-turn, interactive scenarios that better reflect real-world developer workflows. Unlike static benchmarks, it uses a persona-driven simulation to mimic dynamic user interactions and verifies patches using execution-grounded tests at every turn. Testing eleven agents across 72 tasks revealed that performance rankings shift significantly depending on the interaction budget, proving that single-turn evaluations are insufficient for measuring interactive coding capabilities.
items.bottom_line: Single-turn benchmarks are no longer sufficient to accurately rank the performance of interactive AI coding agents.

items.title: Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority
items.one_liner: System One legal decision models outperform generative LLMs in knowing when to abstain from missing legal authority while operating at a fraction of the cost.
items.summary: Researchers explore System One decision models built on large language models that output calibrated probabilities instead of text to verify legal authority cost-effectively. Testing these models against generative LLMs on an extended CaseHOLD benchmark with missing correct holdings revealed that generative LLMs still pick an incorrect option in 38-86% of items when no option is correct, whereas the most cautious decision model does so only 30% of the time. While matching the best generative LLM's accuracy on standard CaseHOLD at one-fifty-fifth of the cost, these decision models successfully identify when mandatory legal authority is absent and can abstain. Distilling these probabilities into smaller models like Qwen3-8B produces well-calibrated local legal verification tools.

Cost ratio: 1/55 of generative LLM cost
items.bottom_line: System One decision models provide a more reliable, cost-effective alternative to generative LLMs for legal citation checking by properly handling cases where correct authority is missing.

items.title: Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents
items.one_liner: Behavioral Localization targets critical trajectory positions to train concise, highly effective soft prompts for tool-using AI agents.
items.summary: Researchers propose 'Behavioral Localization' as a technique for robust soft skill adaptation in tool-using agents, addressing the limitation that learning from entire successful trajectories introduces unnecessary behavioral drift. By comparing a frozen agent with and without a given text skill, the method identifies specific trajectory positions where the skill alters the token distribution and boosts success likelihood. Supervising a short soft prompt using only the top 10% of these behaviorally relevant positions captures 96.12% of the total positive skill gain. Experiments on SpreadsheetBench with a frozen Qwen3.6-35B-A3B agent show that selective supervision increases success rates significantly compared to full trajectory training or on-policy baselines.
items.bottom_line: Isolating the top 10% of behaviorally relevant trajectory positions allows efficient soft prompt supervision for tool-using agents without full-trajectory noise.

items.title: Recursive Self-Improvement on a Budget: Scoring Code Edits Before They Run
items.one_liner: Scoring code edits before execution via steerable linear readouts enables efficient recursive self-improvement for coding agents on a budget.
items.summary: Researchers explore budget-friendly recursive self-improvement methods for coding agents by scoring proposed code edits before execution. The approach fits linear readouts on a parent's steering-split solve rate alongside eight diff coordinates derived from a small set of evaluations, then freezes those coefficients. Huxley-Gödel Machine selection uses Thompson sampling on previously evaluated nodes' steering counts to select parent nodes for expansion. Evaluated across HumanEval+ and Polyglot benchmarks using GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.5, the selection method reliably matches or outperforms parent-rate ablations and calibration-best edits on held-out test instances, achieving 85.1% and 86.5% respectively.
items.bottom_line: Predictive scoring of code edits using Thompson sampling and steering-split metrics allows coding agents to self-improve efficiently without exhaustive evaluations.

items.title: TIDE: Tree-Induced Fine-Grained Diagnostic Evaluation from Model Behaviors
items.one_liner: TIDE uses decision-tree induction on model behaviors to uncover fine-grained capabilities hidden by aggregate LLM benchmarks.
items.summary: Researchers have proposed Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation (TIDE), a method that recasts LLM diagnostic evaluation as behavior-driven decision-tree induction to perform fine-grained capability diagnosis. TIDE recursively constructs a hierarchical capability tree from benchmark samples and model scores using an LLM judge to propose candidate splits and behavior-based information gain. Applying TIDE across five models and four benchmarks revealed capability contrasts previously hidden at the aggregate level, such as Claude Opus 4.6 outperforming GPT-5.4 in microeconomic market reasoning while trailing in contract law reasoning.
items.bottom_line: Aggregate benchmark scores hide critical capability variations across models, which behavior-driven decision-tree evaluation can expose.

items.title: DiffResearch: Accelerating Deep Research with Diffusion Language Models
items.one_liner: Diffusion language models can replace autoregressive backbones in multi-agent research systems to achieve massive latency reductions.
items.summary: DiffResearch is a new multi-agent framework that replaces traditional autoregressive language models with diffusion language models (dLLMs) to accelerate deep research tasks. By using a diffusion backbone, the system achieves a 6x speedup in end-to-end latency while maintaining report quality. The framework also introduces 'dFast,' a decomposition mode that extracts subqueries before full generation is complete, further optimizing performance for interactive research.
items.bottom_line: Diffusion-based language models offer a significant performance advantage over autoregressive models for complex, multi-step agentic research workflows.

items.title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
items.one_liner: LLMs that correctly refuse harmful requests in text frequently execute unsafe tool calls when given tool access.
items.summary: Researchers investigated whether large language model refusal behaviors in text transfer to tool use by testing five models across a benchmark of 2,304 prompts in text-only and tool-enabled settings. They found that requests refused in text frequently resulted in unsafe tool calls, with divergence occurring in 10% to 52% of harmful requests under standard tool-enabled prompting. A refusal-associated direction was identified in the models' residual streams, where lower activation predicted unsafe tool calls, though safety steering at high strengths degraded output quality or suppressed benign tool use.
items.bottom_line: Text-based safety refusals do not reliably transfer to tool-calling agents, necessitating direct safety evaluations of agent actions.

items.title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development
items.one_liner: GenXR-Bench is a new benchmark evaluating coding agents on interactive extended reality software development.
items.summary: Researchers introduced GenXR-Bench, the first end-to-end benchmark for evaluating coding agents in interactive extended reality (XR) software development. GenXR-Bench comprises 112 expert-authored tasks spanning feature implementations, bug repairs, and application generation within dynamic 3D physical environments. Evaluating 10 models on the benchmark revealed that the strongest configuration achieved only 50.9% overall Pass@1, with failure analyses highlighting recurring agent misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles and embodied interaction semantics.
items.bottom_line: Current coding agents struggle with interactive extended reality development, achieving a maximum Pass@1 score of 50.9% on the GenXR-Bench testbed.

items.title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination
items.one_liner: Using continuous latent tokens for theory-of-mind reasoning improves multi-agent coordination more effectively than text-based descriptions.
items.summary: ToM2Vec is a new approach for multi-agent coordination that uses continuous latent tokens to represent a partner's 'theory-of-mind' (ToM) rather than relying on text-based descriptions. By training these tokens to match a partner's actual thoughts, agents can better reason under uncertainty and improve collaboration in competitive and mixed-motive environments. The researchers found that latent reasoning significantly outperforms text-based reasoning and generalizes to unseen model families.

items.bottom_line: Latent reasoning tokens are critical for effective multi-agent coordination, as they capture partner states more accurately than natural language descriptions.

items.title: AgentPhishing: A Benchmark of LLM Email Agents Under Adaptive Attack
items.one_liner: A new benchmark called AgentPhishing reveals that LLM email agents are highly susceptible to persuasive phishing attacks adapted to their specific behavior.
items.summary: Researchers introduced AgentPhishing, a new benchmark designed to evaluate LLM email agents under adaptive persuasive attacks. The study developed PhishOpt to optimize reusable email-generation skills against individual agents while adhering to fixed benchmark and realism constraints. Evaluating nine agents revealed that while they handled standard phishing emails safely, four exhibited phishing-detection rates below 10% and malicious-request compliance rates exceeding 45% against adaptive attacks. The findings demonstrate that conventional phishing evaluations are insufficient for inferring the actual safety of autonomous agents dealing with persuasive malicious requests.
items.bottom_line: Standard phishing evaluations fail to capture the true vulnerability of autonomous LLM agents when confronted with adaptive, persuasive social engineering.

items.title: AgentMonopoly: Behavioral Patterns and Persona Control in LLM Agents
items.one_liner: Evaluating LLM agents in a Monopoly-style environment shows that persona instructions alter language and some actions, but fail to govern all strategic decisions consistently.
items.summary: Researchers studied behavioral patterns and persona control in LLM agents using AgentMonopoly, a multi-agent simulation environment where models communicate, trade properties, and make strategic decisions. Testing various model families and sizes demonstrated that larger models do not consistently win more games, and that individual strategies regarding trading and rent management differ significantly. Assigning specific personas altered the agents' language and certain actions, but persona adherence was inconsistent across all decisions. The open-source environment provides infrastructure to further analyze and verify how LLM agents execute persona-following behaviors beyond mere text generation.
items.bottom_line: Assessing LLM agent safety and persona adherence requires evaluating concrete actions and outcomes rather than relying solely on generated text.

items.title: D-Skill: Distilling Teacher Knowledge through Agent Skills
items.one_liner: D-Skill distills frontier model behavior into natural-language instructions, providing an efficient, weight-free alternative to standard distillation.
items.summary: Researchers propose D-Skill, a knowledge distillation framework that treats teacher models as black boxes to transfer capabilities to smaller student models via interpretable natural-language skills. By analyzing paired rollouts and consolidating behavioral divergences offline without label requirements or model weight updates, D-Skill bridges 75%-95% of the teacher-student performance gap. The approach outperforms one-epoch SFT baselines while reducing student inference costs by 5.7x to 8.3x per task.

items.title: Fig: Automated Multiagent Behavior Elicitor
items.one_liner: Fig automates behavioral testing for multi-agent LLM systems by actively mutating environment rules and game engines.
items.summary: Researchers developed Fig (Finding Interactions in Games), an agentic system that performs targeted interventions on game environments to evaluate multi-agent social behaviors. Fig takes natural language descriptions, breaks them down into sub-behaviors, and modifies game engines, instructions, and contexts to elicit behaviors like deception and cooperation. Tested across six scenarios, Fig increased target behavior attempt rates by 10.9% on average compared to matched control games. The system demonstrates how multi-agent environments can be systematically used for reproducible behavior evaluation.

items.title: Scanning AI Assets: Catching What SCA and SAST Might Miss
items.one_liner: Traditional code scanners miss malicious intent hidden in AI agent skills and plugins, necessitating specialized intent-based security analysis.
items.summary: Standard application security tools like SCA and SAST fail to protect AI development workflows because they do not evaluate the semantic instructions contained in agent skills, plugins, and Agent Package Manager manifests. These AI assets encode instructions that dictate agent behavior, leaving a blind spot that attackers can exploit using prompt injection, hidden text instructions, and obfuscated payloads. Recent research demonstrated that cloaked malicious skills could evade over 90% of static scanners across multiple tests while successfully executing credential theft and data exfiltration inside production coding agents like Claude Code and Codex.
items.bottom_line: Conventional AppSec scanners fail to catch prompt-based threats in AI agent skills and packages, leaving workflows vulnerable to sophisticated evasion techniques.

items.title: How I Found a $113,337 AF_ALG Linux Local Privilege Escalation Before Copy Fail
items.one_liner: A retrospective look at uncovering a $113,337 Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw in the AF_ALG cryptographic subsystem via unprivileged socket APIs.
items.summary: Security researcher Muhammad Alifa Ramdhan details the discovery of CVE-2025-39964, a critical race condition vulnerability in the Linux kernel's AF_ALG cryptographic subsystem that earned a $113,337 reward via Google's kernelCTF. Exploiting out-of-bounds access stemming from how AF_ALG handles inputs across unprivileged sockets, an ordinary user can escalate privileges to root or achieve container escape. Present in the kernel since 2011, this vulnerability preceded the widely known 'Copy Fail' flaw but highlights the same underlying kernel attack surface.
items.bottom_line: Unprivileged access to the Linux kernel's AF_ALG subsystem harbors deep race condition vulnerabilities capable of full privilege escalation and container escape.

items.title: Encryption isn’t enough to protect data wherever it goes
items.one_liner: Vaultless, keyless pseudonymization protects data across cloud and AI workflows by replacing sensitive values with realistic substitutes, removing central vaults as single points of failure.
items.summary: Traditional cybersecurity policies rely on database encryption, network security, and access controls, but fail to protect data once decrypted and processed across cloud platforms, analytics tools, and AI pipelines. Because data must be read to be used, breaches or future quantum decryption can expose sensitive plaintext information. To mitigate this risk without stalling operations, policymakers and organizations are turning to vaultless, keyless pseudonymization. This approach replaces sensitive identifiers like names, social security numbers, and payment cards with structurally valid substitutes, eliminating central vaults as single points of failure and rendering stolen data useless to threat actors.
items.bottom_line: Encryption leaves decrypted data vulnerable during processing, making vaultless pseudonymization necessary to strip stolen data of its value.

claims.text: Encryption protects data when it is stored or traveling, only partially protects it when it is transmitted, and does not protect data at all when it is processed.

items.summary: A federal judge in Argentina dismissed a criminal investigation into President Javier Milei and his sister Karina Milei concerning their ties to the collapsed cryptocurrency $Libra. Federal judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi dropped the case at prosecutors' request, ruling that the reported events did not constitute a crime and that no criminally relevant deception was proven. The controversy began in February 2025 when President Milei promoted the token on social media, causing its price to surge before crashing and leaving investors with massive losses. While opposition politicians accused the president of executing a cryptocurrency rug pull, Milei maintained that he acted in good faith, deleted the post upon learning details of the project, and stated that investors participated voluntarily.
items.bottom_line: Legal accountability for cryptocurrency promotions by political figures remains difficult to establish when courts rule that social media shares lack proven criminal deception.

items.one_liner: A Bengaluru survey highlights that financial pressures drive seniors to seek work, while widespread age bias in hiring remains a major hurdle.
items.summary: A survey of 306 senior jobseekers conducted by Nightingales Medical Trust in Bengaluru reveals that financial difficulties and family support obligations are primary drivers pushing older adults to seek employment. Although 41.2% considered themselves financially independent, nearly 70% support at least one other person, and 54.2% have actively applied for jobs. Age-related recruitment bias emerged as the leading barrier, with 49% of respondents citing employer preference for younger applicants. Over 73% of respondents held graduate or higher degrees, seeking administrative, teaching, or consultancy roles while emphasizing the need for flexible working hours, respect, and training in basic computer and AI skills.
items.bottom_line: Older jobseekers in Bengaluru face severe age bias in hiring despite high qualifications, with financial responsibilities compelling many retirees back into the workforce.

items.one_liner: An official update on El Nino drought management in India, relevant for regional infrastructure monitoring.
items.summary: The Cabinet Sub-Committee on Drought and El Nino conditions in Hyderabad held its first meeting to formulate a comprehensive, department-wise action plan to protect drinking water, irrigation, electricity, and rural employment. Chaired by Deputy Chief Minister M. Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju noted that preliminary assessments have already identified 358 drought-affected mandals, and ₹1 crore in emergency funds has been disbursed to each District Collector, with proposals for an additional ₹7,000 crore in special works. Officials are instructed to conduct weekly district-level reviews to monitor groundwater levels and rising temperatures.

items.title: Kerala HC sets aside guidelines for producing accused before judicial officer after court hours
items.one_liner: The Kerala High Court struck down daytime-only restrictions for producing accused individuals before magistrates to protect constitutional rights and investigation timelines.
items.summary: The Kerala High Court has set aside state guidelines that restricted the production of arrested accused persons before judicial officers to daytime hours between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m., except under exceptional circumstances. Hearing a PIL filed by lawyer P.S. Subeesh, a Division Bench of Justices V. Raja Vijayaraghavan and K.V. Jayakumar noted that such restrictions could cause police to delay production until the next morning, violating constitutional mandates and hindering time-sensitive investigations or timely access to legal counsel. The court retained the provision requiring prior intimation to magistrates for post-5 p.m. productions and directed the state government to issue revised guidelines.
items.bottom_line: Police in Kerala cannot delay presenting arrested suspects before magistrates due to arbitrary daytime-only restrictions, ensuring immediate access to legal recourse.

items.title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves
items.one_liner: Use StochIKM to automate high-fidelity individual patient data reconstruction from published oncology Kaplan-Meier curves.
items.summary: StochIKM is a stochastic algorithm designed to automatically reconstruct individual patient data (IPD) from published Kaplan-Meier survival curves with high fidelity. The method employs a vision-capable language model to digitize figures and uses a strict mathematical definition of fidelity—satisfying risk tables, image resolution constraints, and reported medians—as optimization constraints. Evaluated in simulations and across 79 arms from published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces published risk tables and medians more closely than existing alternatives like IPDfromKM.
items.bottom_line: StochIKM uses vision-capable LLMs and strict mathematical constraints to accurately reconstruct individual patient data from Kaplan-Meier curves.

claims.text: We propose StochIKM, a stochastic algorithm that digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets.

items.title: Bridging Number-Theoretic Primality Testing And Algorithmic Optimization: An Adaptive Cryptographic Framework
items.one_liner: Examine the proposed adaptive cryptographic framework for unifying primality testing and machine learning optimization.
items.summary: Modern public-key cryptographic algorithms like RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and ECC rely heavily on the intractability of integer factorization and discrete logarithms, which require generating and verifying massive prime numbers. This research paper presents a comprehensive framework bridging classical number theory with machine learning models and optimization algorithms. The proposed adaptive, arbitrary-precision architecture is dedicated to primality testing, incorporating deterministic and probabilistic testing methods, hardware-level optimizations, and quantum-secured entropy sources.
items.bottom_line: A new cryptographic framework integrates number-theoretic primality testing with machine learning optimization and quantum entropy.

items.title: Inheritance as an Admission Test for LLM Prompt Merge Operators
items.one_liner: A new inheritance-based admission test framework evaluates LLM prompt merge operators by measuring whether child models reliably move toward donor behaviors.
items.summary: Researchers proposed an admission test using inheritance and reference performance to evaluate LLM prompt merge operators. Instead of relying solely on fixed verifiers that saturate, the framework scores agents against a population panel and measures whether merge child models move toward the donor past zero-dose baselines. Testing various operators with gemini-3.1-flash-lite on a negotiation task showed that tactic append operators pass the confidence bound and are admitted, whereas free rewrite operators fail to move the required distance and are rejected. Held-out re-probes confirmed that valid appends successfully generalize across unseen evaluation situations.
items.bottom_line: Rigorous population-based admission tests can systematically filter out ineffective LLM prompt merge operators while validating productive ones.

items.title: To Manipulate or Not: Opinion Dynamics in LLM Interactions
items.one_liner: A study of LLM-to-LLM debates reveals that conversational influence and opinion dynamics depend heavily on the specific model pairings rather than explicit persuasion prompts.
items.summary: Researchers introduced a controlled LLM-to-LLM debate framework to study opinion dynamics during extended conversations on climate change attribution. Using model combinations of GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, the study tracked both explicitly reported positions and turn-by-turn dialogue behavior under varying persuasion instructions. Results showed that opinion dynamics differ significantly depending on the interacting models: same-model interactions narrowed opinion gaps, whereas cross-model interactions widened them. Furthermore, explicit reports and in-dialogue behaviors captured distinct aspects of opinion change, proving that blanket instructions to persuade do not reliably increase influence.
items.bottom_line: Measuring opinion changes in multi-agent LLM interactions requires tracking both dialogue behavior and explicit statements, as model pairings fundamentally alter conversational outcomes.

claims.text: We introduce a controlled LLM-LLM debate framework in which two language-model roles repeatedly discuss a contested topic (climate-change attribution): one is given an assigned stance and, in some conditions, an explicit instruction to persuade, while the other receives no assigned position.

items.title: Where to Find SSH (sshd) Logs on Linux and How to Export Them
items.summary: On Debian and Ubuntu, sshd writes to /var/log/auth.log. On RHEL, Rocky, Alma and CentOS Stream, it writes to /var/log/secure. If neither file exists, your system logs only to the systemd journal. Then the command you want is journalctl -u ssh on Debian-based systems, or journalctl -u sshd on the Red Hat family, Fedora and Arch. SSH is the front door of nearly every Linux server, which is why its logs show up in almost every Linux investigation.
